name: Contrast effect
statement: A judgement is pushed away from whatever was judged just before it, so the same candidate is rated worse after a strong predecessor and better after a weak one.
meaning: This entry is about the judgement version, in which the rating given to the current item moves in the opposite direction to the value of the item seen immediately before. It is a sequential effect. It needs an order, and the item doing the work is usually the most recent one, not the average of everything seen. Two other things carry the same name. One is behavioural contrast in operant conditioning, named by George Reynolds in a 1961 paper in the Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior. The page scans at PubMed Central were rendered and read for this entry. Reynolds ran four adult male White Carneaux pigeons on two-component multiple schedules and measured rates of key pecking, not ratings. Contrast there means the rate of responding during one stimulus moving away from the rate during the other. The remaining sense is perceptual contrast, the psychophysical case in which a stimulus is judged against a recent anchor. Sherif, Taub and Hovland gave that case its standard vocabulary in 1958, and their title names both assimilation and contrast. The two run in opposite directions, and which one appears depends on the setup.

origin.who: Douglas T. Kenrick and Sara E. Gutierres
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: The paper reports three studies. In the field study, 81 male dormitory residents watching a television show with three attractive women in the lead were asked to rate a photograph of an average woman described as a possible blind date for another resident. The abstract says they rated her less attractive than a comparable control group did, and reports that difference as significant. Two further studies with 146 undergraduates are described as showing analogous effects in a controlled laboratory setting. Only the abstract was read, from the Arizona State University record. The full text was not obtained on 21 September 2026. Unpaywall lists no open copy, Semantic Scholar records the digital object identifier as closed, and the PsycNet record page serves no text at all. No condition means or test statistics from the 1980 paper appear here. The name is older than the paper. Sherif, Taub and Hovland used it for anchored psychophysical judgements in 1958, and their PubMed record carries no abstract.

evidence: The field evidence is stronger than the laboratory evidence, which is unusual. Bhargava and Fisman analysed 16 speed dating sessions run in the New York area between 2002 and 2004, in which nearly 500 participants made over 7,000 yes or no decisions. A one point rise in the previous partner's attractiveness on a 1 to 10 scale cut the chance of a yes for the current partner by 1.9 percentage points. That is against an overall willingness to date of 42%. The authors put the pull at 18% of the pull of the same change in the current partner's own attractiveness, and at 31% for male evaluators, who drove nearly all of it. Only the first lag mattered. Attractiveness two and three partners back did not predict the current decision, and a placebo test on future partners found nothing. Hartzmark and Shue applied the same logic to share prices, using 75,897 unique earnings announcements between 1984 and 2013. Moving yesterday's salient surprise from the average of the worst decile to the average of the best was associated with a 55 basis point lower return reaction to today's announcement, holding today's news constant. One standard deviation of yesterday's surprise was worth 16 basis points. In the laboratory, Pegors, Mattar, Bryan and Epstein recruited 32 undergraduates and analysed 30, who rated faces one at a time, alternating attractiveness ratings with hair darkness ratings. The attractiveness of the previous face pushed the current rating down (t(29) = -4.92, p < 0.001) while the previous response pulled it up (t(29) = 2.73, p = 0.011). The contrast came from the stimulus and the assimilation from the response, in the same data.

replication.headline: The sequential judgement effect holds in large pre-registered field data, and the attractiveness branch the name was coined in does not. Radbruch and Schiprowski found the previous candidate's influence across about 37,000 interviews, while Balzarini and colleagues met a pooled effect of d = 0.02 in three pre-registered replications.
replication.detail: Radbruch and Schiprowski used register data from a German study grant admission process, about 29,000 interviews, and the hiring process of a large consulting firm, 8,423 interviews conducted by 357 evaluators. The two datasets together hold about 3,000 evaluators and about 37,000 interviews, and both of those round figures are the authors' own. Candidates were quasi-randomly assigned to evaluators and time slots, and the main specifications were pre-registered at osf.io/t65zq. A candidate was assessed worse when the other candidates given to the same evaluator were stronger, and the immediately preceding candidate mattered about three times as much as the average other candidate. A one standard deviation rise in the previous candidate's quality measure was about 25% as influential in the admission process, and about 45% in the hiring process, as a one standard deviation fall in the candidate's own quality. Candidates following a yes vote were about 15% less likely to get one in admissions and about 40% less likely in hiring. The distortion carried through to the committees. An extra yes vote for the previous candidate in one of two interviews cut the chance of being admitted or hired by about 20% relative to the average. These figures are read from the published Review of Economic Studies article, which is open access. The attractiveness branch did worse, and the case worth noticing is that the original authors had already repeated it themselves. Kenrick, Gutierres and Goldberg ran the paradigm again in 1989 and reported the same decrement, this time for men exposed to centrefolds rating their own partners. Balzarini, Dobson, Chin and Campbell then ran three pre-registered close replications of that 1989 study 2, each powered at 0.95, analysing 223, 263 and 344 participants. Their random effects meta-analysis of the original plus the three replications covered 218 men in the centrefold condition and 227 in the abstract art condition. It gave a weighted mean of d = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.21, 0.24] for partner attractiveness and d = 0.02, 95% CI [-0.22, 0.26] for love. The original figures were d = 0.91 and d = 0.69, from 30 men in total.

study.cite: Radbruch, J., & Schiprowski, A. (2025). Interview Sequences and the Formation of Subjective Assessments. Review of Economic Studies, 92(2), 1226-1256.

limits: The effect is short-ranged. In speed dating only the immediately preceding partner predicted the current decision, and the two before that did not. Radbruch and Schiprowski found the same shape and three things that weaken it: the influence falls as an evaluator works through a sequence, longer breaks between interviews go with lower autocorrelation, and a dissimilar previous candidate contrasts less than a similar one. Experience across past sequences did not mitigate it, and an information treatment the grant programme actually ran turned out to be ineffective. Their simulations of reordering candidates reduce the distortion without removing it. Direction is not guaranteed either. Pegors found the previous response producing assimilation in the same trials where the previous stimulus produced contrast, so a design that fails to separate the two can record either sign. Xia, Leib and Whitney went further in the same task. Showing each face for one second, with 135 subjects analysed in their first experiment, they found the current rating pulled towards the previous face rather than away, with an effect size of 0.042. They read the disagreement with Pegors as a matter of exposure time, since Pegors showed each face for four seconds. On their account a short look gives assimilation and a long look gives a negative aftereffect, and the two do not preclude one another. The speed dating result was almost entirely male, with female evaluators showing no sensitivity to the previous partner. Nothing here establishes the size of the effect in the original 1980 studies, whose full text was not obtained.
misreadings: Simonsohn and Gino's admissions paper is the one most often cited as proof of contrast effects, and it argues the opposite. They studied 9,323 interviews by 31 interviewers and found the score for an applicant fell as the average score already given that day rose (B = -.088, p = .018 in their fullest model). They then tested contrast directly. If contrast drove it, the five specific subscores should move too, and more sharply. None of them did: communication B = -.009, driven B = -.037, teamwork B = -.027, accomplishment B = -.052, interest in the school B = .025, none significant. They concluded that contrast effects were an unlikely explanation and named the pattern narrow bracketing, a reluctance to hand out a fourth high score in one day. Radbruch and Schiprowski treat that finding as a separate phenomenon from theirs and note the difference in scale, 31 evaluators against about 3,000. The second misreading is the media claim. Kenrick and Gutierres's title says beauty becomes a social problem, and the popular version is that watching attractive strangers spoils your own relationship. That is the 1989 extension, and it is the part with three failed pre-registered replications behind it, not the part with 37,000 interviews. The third is treating the three senses of the name as one finding. Reynolds measured how fast pigeons pecked a key under one schedule when the schedule behind a different key changed. Nothing in that record bears on how a person rates a job candidate.

Gutierres, S. E., Kenrick, D. T., & Partch, J. J. (1999). Beauty, dominance, and the mating game: Contrast effects in self-assessment reflect gender differences in mate selection. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 25(9), 1126-1134. Abstract read from the record at Arizona State University. Listed to show where the original authors took the work next, which was self-assessment rather than judgements of other people. No figure from it is used here.

Reynolds, G. S. (1961). Behavioral contrast. Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior, 4(1), 57-71. Cited to show the name is shared. The article is held at PubMed Central as page scans, and the scans were rendered and read for this entry. Source for the four pigeons, the multiple schedules and the definition of contrast used in that literature.

Forth, J. M., & Freeman, H. R. (1997). Contrast effects and ratings of physical attractiveness. Psi Chi Journal of Undergraduate Research, 2(1), 24-27. An undergraduate journal, not indexed by Crossref. Ninety-seven students rated average-looking targets after attractive or unattractive photographs. The positive contrast condition rated the female target lower than the negative contrast condition did, F(1, 93) = 5.45, p = .02, and the male target lower, F(1, 93) = 4.99, p = .03. There was no unexposed control group.
